History: heart failure, palpitations (arrhythmias), stroke (embolic)
Examination: heart failure signs, neurological examination, murmurs
Investigations
FBC: anaemia or polycythaemia
Urea and electrolytes: electrolytes, renal function
ECG: arrhythmia, conduction defects, ischaemia
Echo: LV function, valves
CXR: left ventricular failure

Treatment: diuretics, ACE inhibitors, nitrates, amiodarone (arrhythmias), digoxin (arrhythmias and positive inotropy), beta-blockers (carvedilol), anticoagulation, dual-chamber pacing with or without ICD
Intraoperative management
Invasive monitoring including cardiac output
Keep sinus rhythm, adequate volume, normal SVR
Avoid myocardial depression
Inotropes often needed (dobutamine or milrinone)
Postoperative: HDU or ICU
Rare; right heart failure often dominant
Amyloid infiltration: stiff ventricle and diastolic dysfunction
History: breathlessness, fatigue; examination: heart failure, especially right-sided
Echo: diastolic dysfunction
High-risk anaesthetic
Keep sinus rhythm, load volume, high-normal SVR
Vasodilation, myocardial depression and reduced venous return together cause cardiovascular collapse
Spontaneous ventilation if possible
Ketamine is a good choice (raises contractility and peripheral resistance)
Airway: poor dental hygiene, neck contractures, TMJ dislocation, aspiration (reflux, bulbar dysfunction)
Respiratory: restrictive lung disease from scoliosis, chest infections
Neurological: seizures; sensitive to anaesthetics
Musculoskeletal: hypothermia, difficult positioning, difficult IV access
Cognitive impairment
Group of non-progressive disorders of movement and posture appearing early in life
Due to lesions of the motor pathways in the developing brain
Severity ranges from mild monoplegia to severe spastic quadriplegia
Often with intellectual impairment, developmental delay, speech problems and epilepsy
Incidence 2.5:1000
Causes:
Prenatal: congenital infection (rubella, toxoplasmosis, CMV, herpes), cerebral malformation
Perinatal: asphyxia
Postnatal: IVH, cerebral ischaemia, trauma, non-accidental injury, meningitis
Linked to prematurity and low birth weight
Classified by main motor type:
Spastic: hemiplegia, diplegia or quadriplegia
Ataxic: poor balance, tremor, hypotonia, uncoordinated movement
Dyskinetic (athetoid): involuntary movements (athetosis, dystonia), poor or fluctuating tone
Some have normal intelligence despite severe deformity, but struggle to communicate
Muscle contractures and spasms
Multidisciplinary care: physiotherapy, splints and drugs to control spasm and delay contractures
Antispasmodic drugs:
Central: baclofen (oral or intrathecal), diazepam, vigabatrin, tizanidine; mainly sedative side effects
Peripheral: botulinum toxin type A, dantrolene
Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the motor end-plate; effect about 3 months
Progressive scoliosis may impair breathing or sitting
Reflux and swallowing problems lead to recurrent chest infections
Orthopaedic: muscle releases and transfers, foot or femoral osteotomies; femoral and pelvic osteotomies and scoliosis correction for wheelchair seating
Feeding gastrostomy, fundoplication for reflux, dental rehabilitation
Often many previous admissions; review previous anaesthetic records
Main problems: recurrent chest infections, poor nutrition, seizure control, higher incidence of latex allergy
Often on anticonvulsants or antispasmodics
Position carefully and pad pressure areas
IV access may be hard (scarring, contractures)
Reflux common: often needs rapid sequence induction
Laparoscopic fundoplication reduces postoperative chest complications
Increased secretions and drooling: antisialogogue may help a gas induction
Time fasting around feeding times
Hypothermia in poorly nourished patients: active warming (mattress, forced air, warmed IV fluids)
Suxamethonium:
Patients may be more sensitive, but it is not contraindicated
Extra-junctional ACh receptors found in up to 30% in some studies; others show no extra potassium release
Non-depolarising relaxants:
Less potent, shorter acting due to ACh receptor up-regulation
Offset clinically by a smaller total body water (patients often relatively dehydrated)
Resistance may also relate to anticonvulsants
Pain and muscle spasm can be hard to control
Epidurals are very effective but hard to site with scoliosis
Regional blocks, morphine infusion, oral benzodiazepines also work
IV midazolam may be needed for distressing spasm
Restart feeds and medication early
CKD (not on dialysis): protect renal function, adjust drug doses
ESRF: fluid status, electrolytes and potassium, creatinine, pharmacokinetics, anaemia, IHD risk
Haemodialysis: timing and events of last dialysis, fluid and electrolytes after it, fistula care
Peritoneal dialysis: drain the fluid, check fluid and electrolytes, haemodialysis if needed
Causes: diabetes, hypertension
Acute complications: AEIOU (acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, uraemia)
Chronic complications: IHD, renal bone disease, anaemia
Treatment: fluid restriction; renal replacement therapy changes the acute complications
Haemodialysis: dialyse the day before; check fluid and electrolytes afterwards; fistula care
Peritoneal dialysis: drain, check fluid and electrolytes, haemodialysis if needed
Anaesthetic: altered drug pharmacokinetics; difficult venous access
Optimisation: correct fluid status, electrolytes and uraemia; transfuse for anaemia

text: Watch for hyperkalaemia with transfusion
Creatinine, eGFR and trend: is dialysis adequate?
Screen for and correct complications:
Fluid overload: breathlessness, basal crackles, raised JVP, ankle oedema, hypertension
Fluid restriction target; dialysis regimen, site, dry weight, last session
May instead be fluid depleted from dialysis
Hyperkalaemia: aim K <5.0-5.5; recheck 4 hours after dialysis if unstable or concerned
Metabolic acidosis: check bicarbonate
Anaemia: target Hb 9-10g/dL with EPO
Renal bone disease: hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia
Uraemic platelet dysfunction: consider desmopressin if bleeding risk is high
Uraemic neuropathy
Comorbidities: diabetes, hypertension, IHD or MI (high MACE risk; part of the RCRI)
Most IV induction agents (propofol, etomidate, thiopental) are safe
Thiopental: larger volume of distribution and less protein binding, so reduce the dose
Many patients behave as if hypovolaemic at induction; uraemia and antihypertensives make hypotension more likely
Induction agents may have exaggerated CNS effects (uraemia disrupts the blood-brain barrier)
RSI if indicated:
Suxamethonium can be given if potassium is less than 5 mmol/L; potassium release is not exaggerated in CKD
Or rocuronium for fast onset
Volatile elimination does not depend on the kidneys
Some avoid sevoflurane (fluoride, compound A), though there is no evidence of extra renal harm in renal disease; some avoid it for long cases
Volatiles can depress cardiac output too much
TIVA is an option
Non-depolarising relaxants: choose by clearance route
Reduce the first dose and guide later doses with a nerve stimulator
Vecuronium and rocuronium may be excreted more slowly; mivacurium, atracurium and cisatracurium clearance does not depend on the kidneys
Laudanosine (from atracurium and cisatracurium) may accumulate; no neuromuscular effect, but high levels can cause seizures
Blunted sympathetic activity limits compensatory vasoconstriction: small blood loss, starting IPPV, sudden position change or myocardial depression can drop BP sharply
Opioids are useful: no myocardial depression and less volatile needed; choose those without active metabolites or renal excretion
Morphine and pethidine (meperidine) form neurotoxic metabolites cleared by the kidney (morphine-3-glucuronide, norpethidine)
Morphine-6-glucuronide is more potent than morphine and can accumulate, causing profound respiratory depression
Hydromorphone-3-glucuronide can accumulate; hydromorphone usable with monitoring and dose reduction
Fentanyl has no active metabolites, but its elimination half-life may be longer
Alfentanil, remifentanil and sufentanil have no active metabolites
Avoid NSAIDs: worsen hypertension and oedema, raise cardiovascular risk
Give fluids carefully: overload risk
If still passing urine, aim for at least 0.5 mL/kg/h
Use Hartmann's (contains 4 mEq/L potassium) and other potassium-containing fluids with caution; normal saline is an option but risks hyperchloraemic acidosis
Best maintenance fluid is debated: 0.9% saline has no potassium but can worsen acidosis
Avoid hypercapnia: respiratory acidosis worsens acidaemia, depresses the circulation and raises potassium
Consider an arterial line
CVP often very helpful for fluids, as even mild renal impairment tolerates volume poorly; right atrial or pulmonary artery pressure chosen by cardiopulmonary disease
TOE or FloTrac are alternatives
Uraemic platelet dysfunction can increase blood loss
With renally excreted relaxants (e.g. rocuronium), monitor and reverse in all
Kidneys clear about 50% of neostigmine and about 75% of edrophonium and pyridostigmine
Their half-lives lengthen more than the relaxants', so recurarisation is less likely
Check electrolytes, urea, creatinine and haematocrit
Chest X-ray if pulmonary oedema is a concern
Consider uraemic coagulopathy if bleeding
Fentanyl PCA rather than morphine PCA
Dialysis regimen, access site, dry weight, residual urine output
Optimise dialysis adequacy:
Fluid status (may be depleted after dialysis)
Electrolytes
Last dialysis: best 12-24hr before elective surgery; arrange it in advance
Note recent dialysis problems (e.g. hypotension)
Wait 4-6h after haemodialysis before surgery, for fluid equilibration and heparin metabolism
Recheck electrolytes 4hrs after dialysis
Risk of dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
Regional anaesthesia:
Consider residual heparin
Neuraxial: keep intravascular volume adequate to limit hypotension
Brachial plexus block suits AV fistula surgery: analgesia, abolishes vasospasm and vasodilates
Dialysis alters drug pharmacokinetics
AV fistula:
No BP cuff on the fistula arm; cuff and drip then share an arm, so use an anti-reflux valve
Save veins for future access: no venepuncture in the non-dominant arm or the upper dominant arm
Dialysis catheters:
Temporary dialysis catheters may be used for IV access if other access fails (discouraged):
Central access may be hard with a tunnelled or temporary catheter, or many previous ones, due to central vein stenosis
Venous access:
Often difficult; avoid the antecubital fossa if a fistula or graft is planned
Avoid femoral lines if renal transplant planned, and subclavian lines if dialysis planned (stenosis risk)
Fluids: no renal function means a narrow margin between too little and too much
Most arrive with a contracted ECF volume: mild hypovolaemia after dialysis worsens hypotension from drugs and autonomic neuropathy
Minor surgery: replace insensible losses only (not Holliday-Segar)
CVP often useful
Consider a small bag (e.g. 100ml normal saline) to avoid accidental boluses
Positioning: poor nutrition makes skin bruise and slough easily; pad elbows, knees and ankles
Protect the fistula at all costs: pad well, do not tuck the arm if possible, check the thrill during surgery
Haemodialysis can restart 1 day after surgery; consider heparin-related bleeding
Neurological symptoms from cerebral oedema
Risk factors:
First dialysis
Predialysis urea > 175mg/dL or > 60mmol/L
CKD rather than AKI
Extremes of age
Existing neurological disease (head injury, stroke, epilepsy)
Other causes of cerebral oedema (hyponatraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, malignant hypertension)
Leaky blood-brain barrier (sepsis, vasculitis, TTP or HUS, encephalitis, meningitis)
Mechanism: rapid urea removal lowers plasma osmolality; urea in brain cells cannot equilibrate in time (takes hours), so water shifts into the brain
Features (during or just after haemodialysis, or starting CRRT):
Early: headache, disorientation, blurred vision, dizziness, nausea, cramps, anorexia
Late: confusion, seizures, coma, death
Self-limiting, usually settles within hours
Prevention: slow urea removal when starting dialysis
Management: treat headache and nausea; slow blood flow or stop dialysis; support during seizures; raising osmolality gradually with mannitol or hypertonic saline 3% is controversial
Drain peritoneal fluid before anaesthesia (protects breathing and gastric emptying)
Can usually omit 24-48h of dialysis
Restart after surgery; may need haemodialysis after abdominal surgery
Grade severity with Child-Pugh score; review complications system by system
Liver functions to remember:
Breakdown: bilirubin, ammonia
Synthesis: albumin, clotting factors (coagulopathy), glucose
Portal hypertension: ascites (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), hypersplenism, varices
Reduced drug clearance
Pringle manoeuvre: manual occlusion of the hepatoduodenal ligament (pedicle) to limit hepatic inflow; can also be done with a clamp or a tightened silicone tube
Varices: TEE contraindicated; pass NG tubes carefully
Advantages:
Opioid sparing
Fewer respiratory complications
Increased hepatic blood flow
Disadvantages:
Coagulopathy may rule it out
Postoperative liver dysfunction can cause coagulopathy that affects catheter removal
Neuraxial block worsens vasodilation and hypotension
LAST risk, especially with long infusions, as local anaesthetics are metabolised by the liver
Child C or MELD > 14: high mortality (>50%); avoid intervention unless life-saving
Child B or MELD > 8-14: higher risk; weigh the indication for surgery carefully
Child A or MELD ≤ 8: low perioperative mortality
Child-Pugh points are summed:
5 or 6 = class A: low operative mortality (<5%)
7–9 = class B: moderate (25%)
10–15 = class C: high (>50%)
First used for portosystemic shunt surgery; its variables also predict outcome in all abdominal surgery in liver disease
Other poor prognostic factors: malnutrition, emergency surgery, sepsis, blood loss
Portal hypertension (portal pressure >10 mm Hg): collateral shunts, varices, ascites, splenomegaly
Treatment: transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)
**Gastric and oesophageal varices**
Can bleed **catastrophically**
Even small GI bleeds can trigger or worsen **encephalopathy**, as digested blood greatly raises the bilirubin load on the liver
Treatment: non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol), band ligation or glue, octreotide or terlipressin for acute bleeds
**Careful NG tube insertion; TEE may be contraindicated**
**Splenomegaly**: platelet sequestration causing **thrombocytopaenia**
**Ascites**
Massive ascites raises **intra-abdominal pressure**:
**Aspiration risk**
Splints the diaphragm, reduces FRC, causes atelectasis
Treatment: **sodium and water restriction**, with or without **paracentesis**
Large-volume paracentesis (>5L) drops intra-abdominal pressure fast; blood pools in the abdomen, preload falls and hypotension follows
**Give 100ml 20% HAS per 2.5L of ascites drained** (same for liver transplant with an abdominal drain)
Delayed gastric emptying adds to aspiration risk
**Hyperdynamic circulation**: high CO, low SVR, wide pulse pressure
From portosystemic shunting and poor clearance of vasodilators (nitric oxide)
**Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy**: hidden systolic and diastolic dysfunction and long QT, masked by low SVR and unmasked by surgical stress or clamping
**Hepatopulmonary syndrome**: intrapulmonary arteriovenous shunting
Sign: **platypnoea-orthodeoxia** (breathlessness and hypoxaemia worse **sitting up**, better lying flat)
Test: echo with **agitated saline bubble study**
**Portopulmonary hypertension**: true pulmonary hypertension (high PVR, normal PCWP) caused by portal hypertension; high perioperative mortality
Thrombocytopaenia from hypersplenism
Poor clotting factor synthesis causes **coagulopathy**, mainly the **vitamin K**-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X; PT and APTT prolonged
**Anaemia**: GI blood loss, hypersplenism, haemolysis, malnutrition
Any acute worsening of liver function can cause **hepatorenal syndrome**
Causes: renal hypoperfusion, portal hypertension, intra-abdominal hypertension, nephrotoxins
May need postoperative haemodialysis; poor prognosis
GA vasodilation can cause renal hypoperfusion and pre-renal failure
Secondary hyperaldosteronism: water retention and hyponatraemia, leading to ascites and peripheral oedema
Loop diuretics can cause relative hypovolaemia and hypokalaemia
Spironolactone can cause hyperkalaemia
Low liver and muscle glycogen: perioperative **hypoglycaemia**
Muscle wasting from poor protein synthesis and malnutrition
**Hepatic encephalopathy**
Major feature of acute liver failure; graded by conscious level
Deep coma reflects cerebral oedema and raised ICP; grave prognosis
In chronic disease, triggered by infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte or acid-base upset, sedatives, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, hypotension or high protein intake; or may reflect slow progression
Alcoholic liver disease and haemosiderosis are linked with cardiomyopathy
Alcoholic patients with thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency risk Wernicke's encephalopathy
Focus on **how severe the liver dysfunction is** and **its effects on other organs**
Establish hepatitis B or C status (risk to theatre staff); treat hepatitis of unknown cause as infectious
History and examination:
Compensated disease may be silent or give vague symptoms (malaise, weight loss, dyspepsia); signs may be absent
Look for signs of advanced disease: muscle wasting, spider naevi, pleural effusions, ascites, splenomegaly, encephalopathy
Investigations:
**FBC**: anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, raised white cells with infection
**Renal function**; correct severe **hyponatraemia** or **potassium** problems before surgery
Severe hyponatraemia may explain altered consciousness
Correct slowly, <10 mmol litre−1 in 24 h, to avoid central pontine myelinolysis
**PT** is the best test of synthetic function
Prognostic in acute liver failure and after surgery in chronic disease
Also raised by vitamin K deficiency, DIC and warfarin
Give vitamin K for several days before surgery where possible
**Albumin** is also useful
Raised bilirubin is common; enzyme pattern depends on the cause
ECG; echo if risk of LV dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, valve disease or pulmonary vascular disease; exercise ECG or dynamic LV assessment if significant coronary disease suspected
**Chest X-ray** or ultrasound for **pleural effusions** needing drainage; lung function tests for restrictive or obstructive disease
Elective surgery only if chronic liver disease is **well compensated**
Emergency surgery: **urgent optimisation** of volume status, coagulation, neurological state and infection screen
**Targeted blood components** guided by **thromboelastography** and clotting tests:
FFP if PT >1.5 times control
Platelets if count <50 000 mm−3
Cryoprecipitate usually only if fibrinogen <1.0 g litre−1
Recombinant factor VIIa increasingly used for prevention and treatment of bleeding; also tranexamic acid and desmopressin
**Avoid sedative premedication** (may precipitate encephalopathy); H2 antagonist (e.g. ranitidine) premedication advisable
Decision by severity:
Child-Pugh A or B: proceed; monitor and treat encephalopathy, coagulopathy, metabolic and electrolyte problems
Child-Pugh C: prefer non-surgical options; defer necessary elective surgery until improved
Acute hepatic dysfunction: defer elective surgery until improved
Contraindications to elective surgery:
Acute alcoholic hepatitis
Acute viral hepatitis
Child-Pugh C cirrhosis
Fulminant hepatic failure
Severe chronic hepatitis
Severe coagulopathy (**PT prolonged >3 seconds** despite vitamin K; **platelets <50,000/mm3**)
Severe extrahepatic complications
Acute renal failure
Cardiomyopathy, heart failure
Hypoxaemia
Goal: **maintain hepatic blood flow and oxygen delivery**
Hypoperfusion or hypoxaemia can injure hepatocytes and cause decompensation
With portal hypertension, **liver supply depends on hepatic arterial flow**
**All anaesthetic techniques** can lower MAP and so hepatic blood flow
Other factors that reduce hepatic flow: **surgical traction, positive pressure ventilation, hypocapnia, alpha agonists, laparoscopy**
Monitoring for major surgery:
Arterial and central venous pressure; arterial line for gases, lactate, glucose, electrolytes and coagulation
Core temperature, neuromuscular monitoring, urine output
TEE can help, but **probe placement is contraindicated with oesophageal varices**, as are NG tubes and oesophageal temperature probes; a PA catheter may be needed instead
Drugs: careful use matters more than choice
Suggested: IV induction with propofol and remifentanil; usually modified **RSI** with cricoid pressure and rocuronium 1 mg kg−1; maintain with oxygen, air, desflurane and remifentanil infusion
Propofol TCI is an alternative, useful for endoscopy and radiology; propofol clearance is not much affected by liver disease
**Atracurium** preferred for maintenance of neuromuscular block
Fluids and circulation:
Large-bore IV access is mandatory; warm all fluids; rapid infuser for major surgery
Guide fluids by haemodynamics, blood loss and urine output
Use vasopressors (metaraminol, phenylephrine, noradrenaline) for hypotension only once filling is optimised
Keep circulating volume and haemodynamics right to maintain urine output; loop diuretics or mannitol occasionally
Antioxidants for renal protection remain experimental
Colloids may work better than crystalloids with ascites
Background 5−10% dextrose at 50–100 ml h−1 prevents hypoglycaemia and guards against rises in plasma sodium
IV induction agents:
Thiopental: reduce dose (more unbound drug from low plasma proteins; longer distribution half-life and action)
Propofol: more sensitive to sedative and cardiorespiratory depression; reduce dose
Etomidate: safe, little advantage over thiopental
Chronic alcohol use may raise requirements; use all IV agents with care
Neuromuscular blockers:
Suxamethonium: slower breakdown from low pseudocholinesterase, rarely a problem in practice
Apparent resistance to non-depolarising blockers (larger volume of distribution or altered protein binding)
Vecuronium and rocuronium: prolonged elimination in severe disease
Atracurium and cisatracurium: suitable, not reliant on the liver
Laudanosine (seizure risk) is lower with cisatracurium because of its higher potency; unlikely to matter clinically
Always monitor neuromuscular function
Opioids:
Morphine: slower elimination (lower hepatic flow and extraction); morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in renal failure; best avoided in decompensated disease (may trigger encephalopathy)
Fentanyl: fine in low doses intraoperatively (no active metabolite, renally excreted); accumulates with large or repeated doses
Alfentanil: slower elimination, larger volume of distribution, less protein binding (low alpha-1-acid glycoprotein)
Remifentanil: ideal; broken down by tissue and red cell esterases, which are preserved in severe liver disease (unlike plasma esterases)
Volatile agents:
All lower CO and MAP, and so liver blood flow
Isoflurane, sevoflurane and desflurane have minimal hepatic metabolism and are safe
Desflurane is probably best: least metabolised, fastest emergence, relatively preserves hepatic blood flow (little effect on the hepatic arterial buffer response) and CO
IV PCA with fentanyl (sometimes morphine) is well tolerated in compensated disease
Fentanyl bolus 10 mcg, lockout 10 min, no background infusion
Regional analgesia reduces systemic needs; check coagulation first
TAP blocks or local infiltration recommended
Epidural only with extreme caution, and only if INR is <1.5 and platelets >100 000 mm−3
Clotting factors are not routinely given just to allow an epidural
IM or SC injections risk haematoma
NSAIDs not recommended (GI bleeding, platelet dysfunction, nephrotoxicity)
Paracetamol not contraindicated; use with care and monitor liver function
Plan ICU for advanced liver disease
Postoperative ventilation sometimes appropriate, but usually stop sedation early so neurology can be assessed
Signs of decompensation: worsening encephalopathy, jaundice, ascites
Continue invasive monitoring and careful fluids to avoid renal failure
Keep monitoring coagulation and watch for bleeding
Remove intravascular catheters early (higher catheter sepsis risk)
Bleeding risk
**Neuraxial and deep peripheral nerve blocks contraindicated**; nasal airways contraindicated
PT and APTT
Mixing studies
DIC screen
Refer to haematology
Congenital: may first present in adulthood with a trigger
Acquired:
Reduced factor synthesis
Increased consumption
Substances that interfere with factor function
Common causes:
**Liver disease**
Standard clotting screen misleading (pro- and anticoagulants both low); **ROTEM** is better
Give **vitamin K 10mg** daily, with or without FFP 15ml/kg
**DIC**: sepsis, malignancy
Autoimmune disease (SLE, RA)
Drugs
Malabsorption causing vitamin K deficiency
**INR <1.5** before surgery or line insertion
Low-risk procedures: <2.0 (e.g. compressible peripheral lines, ultrasound-guided femoral access if low risk)
High-risk procedures: **normal INR, i.e. <1.2/1.3** (e.g. **neurosurgery, neuraxial**)
**PT <19.8s (<1.5 times normal)**
**APTT <53.4s (<1.5 times normal)**
Low-risk procedures: <1.8 times normal, e.g. 64s
Surgical haemostasis is paramount
Correct coagulopathy: **prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)**
Blood conservation and preparing for bleeding: **tranexamic acid (TXA)**; avoid the lethal diamond
Technique: **neuraxial and deep peripheral nerve blocks contraindicated**
Airway: **avoid nasal intubation and oropharyngeal airways** in severe coagulopathy (risk of airway bleeding that cannot be compressed)
Types:
Haemophilia A: X-linked recessive defect in factor VIII activity
Severe (spontaneous bleeding): factor VIII <2%
Moderate: 2-5%
Mild (bleeds only after trauma): 5-30%
Haemophilia B (Christmas disease): X-linked recessive defect in factor IX activity
Affects males; females are carriers but can have mild disease
Female homozygotes die in utero
History: bleeding into muscles, joints and internal organs
Examination: signs of bleeding or bruising
Investigations:
Bleeding time normal
APTT prolonged
INR normal
Fibrinogen normal
Specific factor levels reduced
von Willebrand factor normal
Discuss with haematologist
Give recombinant factor as needed:
Aim for factor levels of 50-100% before surgery
Maintain levels for 2-7 days after the procedure
Minimise blood loss and transfusion
Avoid antiplatelets and anticoagulants
Avoid IM injections
Mild bleeding risk:
DDAVP 0.3mcg/kg over 30min
Tranexamic acid 20mg/kg IV over 5 min, three times daily
Moderate to severe bleeding risk:
Replace with recombinant factors, maintained for 2-7 days after surgery
Cryoprecipitate (factor VIII) and FFP (factor XI) only in emergencies
Monitor for bleeding
Close joint care with haematology
von Willebrand factor: protein for platelet adhesion that also carries factor VIII
Deficiency causes:
Factor VIII deficiency
Abnormal platelet adhesion
Abnormal vascular endothelium
Autosomal dominant inheritance
Type 1 (90% of cases): reduced amount of vWF; mild or no symptoms; heterozygous
Type 2 (9%): abnormal vWF function; 4 subtypes (A, B, N, M)
DDAVP contraindicated in 2B (gain-of-function defect: risk of low platelets and thrombosis)
Type 3 (1%): like type 1 but severe symptoms; homozygous; autosomal recessive
History: epistaxis, bruising, haemarthrosis, haematoma, menorrhagia
Platelet count normal
APTT increased
Factor VIII level decreased
vWF level decreased
Bleeding time increased
Platelet function assay time increased
Consult haematologist
Test DDAVP response (0.3mcg/kg IV over 30min), measuring vWF before and after
Responders: **DDAVP** for prophylaxis and bleeding
Non-responders: **factor VIII concentrate or cryoprecipitate**
**Tranexamic acid 20mg/kg IV three times daily** can also be used
Multidisciplinary care with haematology involved
Avoid external cephalic version, ventouse and mid-cavity forceps
Gestational thrombocytopenia (70-80%)
Diagnosis of exclusion; cause unclear (possibly too little thrombopoietin plus higher consumption and turnover)
Usually late 2nd or 3rd trimester
Normal count before pregnancy; recovers within 2 months after delivery
90% stay above 100 (mild); moderate 50-100; severe below 50
Usually no symptoms; no risk to mother or baby; no treatment or special mode of delivery needed
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
About 4% of pregnant women with low platelets
Any trimester; commonest cause of low platelets in the 1st and 2nd trimester
Platelets below 100 × 10^9/L; may bruise easily
Antibodies usually present, but their absence does not exclude ITP
Platelets below 50: oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (note reads "x10/day"), started a week before planned delivery, first line
Emergency caesarean: IVIG 1 g/kg plus platelet transfusion (platelets alone are rapidly consumed)
Pre-eclampsia and HELLP (platelets below 100,000/ul needed for the diagnosis)
Dexamethasone 10 mg 12-hourly, 2-4 doses before delivery and 2 doses after
Worsening haemolysis, thrombocytopenia or renal failure: plasmapheresis
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
DIC
Other causes
Reduced production: marrow failure, folate or B12 deficiency, iron deficiency
Increased destruction: TTP, haemolytic uraemic syndrome; infection (HIV, hepatitis B or C, sepsis); autoimmune (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome); drugs (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)
Congenital: von Willebrand disease type 2b

Warfarin: displaced from protein binding, effect increased
Lithium: levels can rise; monitor
Gout: indomethacin
Dysmenorrhoea: mefenamic acid
Postpartum: naproxen
Children: ibuprofen, diclofenac
Surgical concerns: more bleeding; bone healing (especially spinal fusion)
Rapid absorption from the small bowel
Highly protein bound, small volume of distribution; can displace other highly bound drugs (e.g. warfarin)
Hepatic metabolism; inactive products excreted in urine and bile
Phenylbutazone:
Potent anti-inflammatory
Restricted to hospital use in ankylosing spondylitis because of agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia
Highly protein bound (interactions); can impair liver function, cause rash and sodium and water retention
Tenoxicam:
Can be given IV for rapid onset
Long elimination half-life (72 hours): once daily, long acting
These become drawbacks if side effects occur
Meloxicam:
Tablets and suppositories
Limited preferential COX-2 selectivity, quoted as 3 to 50 times more potent against COX-2
At 7.5 mg/d, fewer GI side effects than diclofenac; renal side effects similar to other NSAIDs
Common starting doses
PO tramadol 25-50 mg three times daily
PO morphine 2.5-5 mg 4-6 hourly plus as needed
PO oxycodone 2-5 mg 4-6 hourly plus as needed
SC fentanyl 25 mcg 4 hourly as needed
Breakthrough oral dosing
Immediate-release dose = 1/6th or 10-20% of the total daily dose, every 4-6 hours
Common palliative order: PO morphine X mg every 4 hours plus every 4 hours as needed (regular and PRN doses can be the same)
Switching to a transdermal patch
For persistent severe chronic pain with stable requirements in opioid-tolerant patients (e.g. oral morphine equivalent dose, OMED, of at least 30 mg/day for more than 72 hours)
Continue the previous analgesia for 12 hours
Breakthrough: immediate-release 1/6th of total daily dose every 4 hours to 1/10th every 2 hours (q4H to q2h)
Increase patch strength only after 2x 72 hour applications (once levels have stabilised)
Nausea and vomiting
Mild: one PRN agent is usually enough
IV ondansetron 4-8 mg 8 hourly
IV metoclopramide 10 mg 6-8 hourly
Moderate to severe: regular round-the-clock dosing of at least one agent; alternatives include dexamethasone and prochlorperazine
Previous severe nausea and vomiting: regular dosing of at least one agent for the first 24 hours, reviewed daily
Ileus and constipation
Laxatives
Targin may help opioid-related ileus (often colicky pain)
Pruritus
Mild: calamine lotion
Moderate to severe: first-generation antihistamines
PO chlorpheniramine 4 mg 6 hourly
IM promethazine 25 mg 6 to 12 hourly
Golden rule: when switching opioids, always convert to oral morphine first
Oral opioids, factor to PO morphine
PO codeine 0.13
PO tramadol 0.2 (PO tramadol 50 mg x 0.2 = PO morphine 10 mg)
PO morphine 1
PO oxycodone 1.5 (PO oxycodone 5 mg x 1.5 = PO morphine 7.5 mg)
IV opioids, factor to PO morphine
IV tramadol 0.3
IV pethidine 0.4
IV morphine 3 (IV morphine 1 mg x 3 = PO morphine 3 mg)
IV oxycodone 3
IV fentanyl 300 (IV fentanyl 10 mcg = 0.01 mg x 300 = PO morphine 3 mg)
In chronic use the factor is closer to 120-200 (IV fentanyl 10 mcg = PO morphine 1.2-2 mg)
Transdermal patches, equivalent PO morphine per day
Fentanyl 12 mcg/h: 30 - 60 mg
Fentanyl 25 mcg/h: 60 - 130 mg
Fentanyl 50 mcg/h: 130 - 220 mg
Quick fentanyl rule: multiply by 3 (fentanyl 25 mcg/h x 3 = PO morphine 75 mg/day)
Buprenorphine 5 mcg/h: 9-14 mg
Buprenorphine 10 mcg/h: 18-28 mg
Quick buprenorphine rule: multiply by 2 (5 mcg/h x 2 = PO morphine 10 mg/day)
Transdermal fentanyl worked conversion
100 mg oral morphine per day is about 1 mg (1000 mcg) fentanyl per day (transdermal or IV)
So 60 mg oral morphine per day is about 0.6 mg (600 mcg) fentanyl per day
600 mcg over 24 hours = 25 mcg/h
So 60 mg oral morphine per day is about a 25 mcg/h fentanyl patch
Opiate: a naturally occurring substance with morphine-like actions
Opioid: the wider term, including synthetic drugs with affinity for opioid receptors
Group 1: naturally occurring (opiates), two chemical classes
Phenanthrenes: morphine, codeine, thebaine
Benzylisoquinolines: papaverine
Group 2: semisynthetic (made by modifying natural opioids)
Heroin (diamorphine, diacetylmorphine)
Hydrocodone (dihydrocodeinone), hydromorphone
Oxycodone (dihydrohydroxycodeinone), oxymorphone
Dihydromorphine, dihydrocodeine, morphinone
Buprenorphine (partial agonist)
Naloxone and naltrexone (antagonists)
Group 3: synthetic
Phenylpiperidines: meperidine (pethidine), fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil
Diphenylpropylamines: methadone
Benzomorphans: pentazocine (partial agonist)
Morphinans: levorphanol, butorphanol (partial agonist)
Others: tramadol, tapentadol
Rash after morphine is usually from histamine release
True anaphylaxis to opioids is very rare (< 1%); local reactions from preservatives or histamine are commoner
With a true allergy, choose a structurally different opioid
Groups 1 and 2 are structurally close: avoid all of them if truly allergic to one
Group 3 drugs differ enough to be given without cross-reactivity, and also differ from each other
Pure agonists: full mu binding; best for acute pain
At equianalgesic doses the common parenteral opioids work equally well with similar side effects
Partial agonists: only partial mu binding, so limited use for pain
Agonist-antagonists: kappa agonist, mu antagonist
Ceiling on respiratory depression, but also a ceiling on analgesia, which limits use in acute pain
Act on mu, kappa and delta receptors in brain and spinal cord, mimicking endogenous endorphins
Most potent clinical analgesics are mu agonists
Opioid receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors
IV: fentanyl, morphine, tramadol, pethidine
IM: tramadol, pethidine
SC: fentanyl, morphine
Transdermal: fentanyl patch
Oral: morphine, codeine, tramadol
Onset
More lipid-soluble opioids act faster (easier transfer to the site of action)
Opioids are weak bases; the free-base share depends on pH and pKa, and the free base is more lipid-soluble
All are partly bound to plasma proteins (albumin and α1-acid glycoprotein)
Only the unionised, unbound fraction diffuses, so onset depends on both lipid solubility and protein binding
The receptor binds the protonated form, so effect intensity tracks the ionised concentration at the site of action
Offset is mainly by redistribution and hepatic metabolism, not urinary excretion
Liver disease
The usual degree of perioperative liver impairment has little effect on most opioids (liver transplant excepted)
Only severe hepatic failure changes morphine or fentanyl clearance noticeably
Renal failure matters most for meperidine, morphine, hydromorphone and their prodrugs
Hepatic enzymes
Enzyme induction (e.g. early alcoholism) can raise hepatic metabolic capacity
CYP3A4 metabolises many opioids, but the polymorphic CYP2D6 matters more clinically (codeine)
Accumulation
Accumulating opioids show a marked rise in context-sensitive half time with long infusions
Remifentanil is broken down as fast as it is given, so it does not
Dosing scalar: clearance relates best to lean body mass; ideal body weight is a reasonable substitute
Haemorrhagic shock: central clearance and central and second-compartment volumes fall; reduce the dose substantially
Age
Neonates eliminate nearly all opioids more slowly (immature metabolism including CYP450); this normalises within the first year
Elderly need less, mainly from pharmacodynamic sensitivity; kinetic changes (smaller central volume, lower clearance) are minor
Few absolute contraindications apart from hypersensitivity to a specific opioid
Relative contraindications are mostly metabolic, e.g. hydromorphone and morphine half-lives lengthen in renal impairment
Analgesia
IV opioids are the mainstay of surgical pain control, and opioids are the commonest drugs for acute and chronic pain
No analgesic ceiling; adverse effects are the limit
Nociceptive pain usually responds; neuropathic pain may respond poorly and need higher doses
Sedation
High doses alone can cause unconsciousness, but unpredictably: not suitable as sole induction agents and not complete anaesthetics
MAC falls with dose, non-linearly, with a ceiling
Synergy with hypnotics such as propofol lowers the effect-site concentration needed for loss of consciousness; effect on BIS is inconsistent
Dose-dependent EEG changes resemble volatile agents but plateau at high doses
No reliable amnesia
Individual response (benefit and side effects) varies widely, likely genetic and environmental
Lower sympathetic tone and raise vagal tone (central vagal nucleus stimulation): bradycardia and hypotension, mainly CNS mediated
Hypovolaemic patients, or those reliant on high sympathetic tone or catecholamine infusions, are prone to hypotension
Meperidine rarely causes bradycardia and can cause tachycardia (its metabolite normeperidine resembles atropine)
Little or no direct myocardial depression, much less than many IV and inhaled anaesthetics
Overall antiarrhythmic (direct action on cardiac ion currents); conduction problems are rare
High-dose opioids preserve myocardial perfusion and O2 supply-demand as well as or better than volatile techniques
No effect on coronary vasomotor tone or myocardial metabolism, no steal, coronary responsiveness intact
May mimic ischaemic preconditioning (possible cardioprotection); clinical outcome benefit unproven
Mild systemic vasodilation, possibly pulmonary vasodilation
Histamine release with morphine, codeine and meperidine
Fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil and remifentanil do not release histamine, so hypotension is less common
Blunt the stress response: sympathetic (autonomic) and hormonal (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis)
Useful when haemodynamic instability is expected
Respiratory depression: the most serious adverse effect
Mu-mediated, dose-dependent, acting directly on brainstem respiratory centres
Reduced ventilatory response to CO2: higher apnoeic threshold and higher end-tidal CO2
Hypoxic drive is less affected than CO2 response, but supplemental oxygen removes the hypoxic stimulus and can deepen depression
Respiratory rate falls markedly with longer expiration, so minute ventilation falls; tidal volume changes little (slow deep breaths)
Breath interval monitoring is a sensitive measure of fentanyl effect
High doses can stop spontaneous breathing without unconsciousness; patients often breathe when told to
Untreated pain causes shallow breathing and atelectasis, so good opioid analgesia can improve postoperative respiratory function
Naloxone is the standard treatment
Factors that worsen or prolong respiratory depression
Other CNS depressants
Older age (more sensitive, and higher plasma levels per weight-based dose)
Neonates and infants (immature blood-brain barrier lets opioids into the brain easily)
Hypocapnia from hyperventilation; anxious or painful hyperventilating patients can become briefly apnoeic after small IV doses as the apnoeic threshold shifts
Airway reflexes
Potent antitussive; blunt somatic and autonomic responses to airway instrumentation (ETT tolerated without bucking)
Can impair protective airway reflexes
Remifentanil can suppress cough at extubation
IV boluses of fentanyl, sufentanil and alfentanil cause brief cough in up to 50% of patients
Bronchospasm from histamine release (especially morphine)
Muscle and chest wall rigidity
Raised muscle tone; mild forms such as hoarseness in awake patients
Significant rigidity usually starts at or after loss of consciousness
Lowers compliance and FRC and impairs ventilation; vocal cord closure is the main cause of difficult bag-mask ventilation
Raises O2 consumption and ICP
Thought to be central (opioid receptors acting on dopamine and GABA pathways in substantia nigra and striatum), not a direct muscle effect
Prevented by muscle relaxants; reversed by naloxone; thiopental induction doses or small doses of diazepam or midazolam can prevent or treat it
Cerebral blood flow
Little effect in general
With vasodilating anaesthetics or N2O, opioids tend to cause cerebral vasoconstriction and lower CBF
Alone, or with vasoconstricting anaesthetics: no change or a small rise
ICP: minimal effect with controlled ventilation; sedation does not change ICP after head injury
Metabolic rate: neuroexcitation and focal seizure activity can raise regional metabolism
Seizures: no risk at normal doses without epilepsy, but high doses can cause neuroexcitation
Normeperidine (N-demethylated pethidine metabolite) causes myoclonus and seizures; risk higher in renal disease
No clear neuroprotection
PONV: intraoperative opioids are a known risk factor
Stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone via 5-HT3 and dopamine receptors; the vomiting centre itself is depressed
Slower gastric emptying, longer transit, constipation and ileus (spastic immobility via myenteric plexus receptors)
Mu activation: antidiuresis and less electrolyte excretion; kappa activation: diuresis with little electrolyte change
Renal function largely preserved; changes are secondary to systemic and renal haemodynamics
Urinary retention, especially after intrathecal opioids
Dose-dependent reduction in detrusor contraction and urge sensation; may tighten the urethral sphincter
Ureteric tone increases
High-dose intraoperative remifentanil gives a small but significant rise in postoperative pain; fentanyl can too
All potent opioids can probably cause it; ultrapotent ones like remifentanil may carry more risk
Abrupt withdrawal may contribute
Remifentanil at 2.5 ng/ mL for 30 minutes then stopped abruptly: hyperalgesia common
Weaned by 0.6 ng/mL every 5 minutes: no hyperalgesia
Mechanism: sensitisation of pronociceptive pathways, probably NMDA receptor involvement
Prevention
Ketamine (supports NMDA role); other NMDA-active drugs: methadone, buprenorphine, butorphanol, N2O
Parecoxib (COX-2 inhibitor) before remifentanil, suggesting COX-2 involvement
Anaesthetic choice: remifentanil hyperalgesia seen with sevoflurane but not with propofol (one study)
Linked to peripheral and central sensitisation and so to chronic postoperative pain
A persistent problem with opioid analgesia; not caused by histamine, as non-histamine-releasing opioids also cause it
Usually no rash (morphine a possible exception)
Worst after intrathecal or epidural use
Antihistamines may help, possibly through sedation
Naloxone reverses it but also reverses analgesia
Mixed or partial agonists (nalbuphine, butorphanol) are increasingly used: partial mu antagonism with kappa analgesia kept
Maternal opioids reduce fetal heart rate variability
Fetal acidosis increases transfer across the placenta
Limiting opioids to the first stage of labour reduces neonatal effects
Fentanyl and morphine reach breast milk at milk-to-plasma ratios of 2 to 3:1, but newborn exposure is negligible
Thermoregulation: thresholds probably lowered about as much as with volatile agents
Pethidine uniquely stops or reduces shivering
Remifentanil increases postanaesthetic shivering
Miosis: opioids remove inhibition of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, constricting the pupil; reversed by atropine
Normally light excites the nucleus, and hypercarbia, hypoxia and pain inhibit it
Pupillometry may help guide intraoperative opioid dosing
Endocrine: growth hormone, TSH and prolactin increase; LH, testosterone, oestradiol and oxytocin fall; effects on vasopressin and ACTH conflict
Main endocrine problem with misuse: hypogonadism, especially in men
Biliary: sphincter of Oddi tone and bile duct pressure increase, usually with little clinical consequence
No evidence that morphine is contraindicated in acute pancreatitis, despite traditional teaching
Sleep: can disrupt sleep on the first postoperative night; effects on circadian rhythm unclear
Mood: euphoria, dysphoria, mood change
Hallucinations: uncommon but important, possibly from dopamine dysregulation
Evoked potentials: sensory (posterior tibial, median nerve) and motor evoked potentials largely unaffected, so spinal cord monitoring works under opioid anaesthesia
Liver: may reduce ischaemia-reperfusion injury, possibly helpful in liver surgery
Teratogenicity of fentanyl, sufentanil and alfentanil appears minimal in animals
Neonatal abstinence syndrome in babies of mothers with opioid use disorder or on prescribed opioids
Fentanyl, sufentanil and alfentanil at induction help prevent a rise in intraocular pressure
Cancer: epidemiology suggests more recurrence after opioid-based GA than after LA or regional techniques; no direct evidence to change practice
Recognition
a) Oversedation: sedation score 3 or unrousable
b) Hypoventilation: respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute or less
Management
Stop the opioid infusion and other sedating drugs (e.g. midazolam, ketamine)
Support airway and breathing, with intubation and ventilation if needed
IV naloxone 0.4 mg (full dose), up to 2 mg IV for diagnosis, repeated as needed
Observe until awake after naloxone has worn off; consider a naloxone infusion until alert without it (up to >48 h with long-acting opioids)
Renarcotisation: any agonist with a longer half-life than naloxone can cause it
Secondary peaks in plasma level can occur from release out of muscle, lung, fat and gut
Tolerance: a fixed dose gives less analgesia over time, so doses escalate
Dependence: a physiological state shown by withdrawal when the drug is stopped abruptly
Withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, insomnia, sweating, yawning, rhinorrhoea, lacrimation; later fever, chills, myalgia, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, tachycardia
Self-limiting, typically 3–7 days
Addiction: use causing physical, psychological or social harm, continued despite it
Mechanisms: not fully known; genetic, molecular, cellular, physiological and functional factors
Changes in mu receptor density are not essential
Short-term desensitisation probably via receptor phosphorylation by protein kinase C
Also implicated: adenylyl cyclase inhibition, reduced protein kinase A, upregulated cAMP pathway, beta-adrenergic receptor kinase (a GRK that rapidly phosphorylates and desensitises GPCRs)
Differential tolerance: different opioid effects develop tolerance at different rates and degrees
Acute tolerance can develop quickly (e.g. remifentanil), not only with chronic use
Chronic high-dose users are probably tolerant, but the size of the effect on analgesia and respiratory depression is hard to predict
Their risk of overdose and death rises with dose
Classical (naloxone-sensitive, IUPHAR): MOP (mu), KOP (kappa), DOP (delta)
Names: mu from morphine, kappa from ketocyclazocine, delta from vas deferens
NOP: non-classical, a non-opioid member of the family
Clinical opioid analgesia is mainly via MOP
Each receptor has selective peptides cleaved from precursor prohormones
MOP: beta-endorphin (precursor pro-opiomelanocortin, POMC); also endomorphin-1 and endomorphin-2 (precursor unknown)
Beta-endorphin acts at all three classical receptors; endorphin means "endogenous morphine"
DOP: met-enkephalin and leu-enkephalin (precursor pro-enkephalin)
KOP: dynorphin A and dynorphin B (precursor pro-dynorphin)
NOP: nociceptin, or orphanin FQ (N/OFQ) (precursor pre-pro-nociceptin)
MOP receptors are throughout the CNS and in peripheral neural and non-neural tissue
Supraspinal: dense in the periaqueductal grey (PAG)
Opioids block resting GABA inhibition of PAG neurons that project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM)
The RVM then releases its brake on descending inhibitory control, increasing antinociceptive output to the dorsal horn
MOP also in basal ganglia and cerebral cortex
Spinal: substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn; reduce glutamate and substance P release, cutting transmission from C and Aδ fibres
Peripheral receptors drive reduced gut motility, urinary retention and pruritus
Immune cells at inflamed sites can release opioid-like peptides acting on primary sensory neurons
Mood and reward: dopaminergic pathways, especially dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens
All are Gi-coupled GPCRs
Inhibit adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP
Close voltage-sensitive calcium channels and open G-protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels, hyperpolarising the cell
Result: lower neuronal excitability, less impulse transmission and less transmitter release
MOP: analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, nausea and vomiting, reduced gut motility; inhibits acetylcholine release
DOP: analgesia
Agonists also slow the gut and depress breathing, limiting interest; may affect mood and movement
No clinical DOP drugs yet
KOP: analgesia, sedation, psychotomimetic effects, diuresis
Spiradoline and enadoline reached clinical trials but caused diuresis, sedation and dysphoria below analgesic doses
Advantage: no respiratory depression; dysphoria limits use
NOP
Spinal N/OFQ: analgesia at high doses, hyperalgesia and allodynia at low doses
Supraspinal (intracerebroventricular): pronociceptive anti-analgesia by inhibiting endogenous opioid tone
Involved in morphine tolerance (upregulated in morphine-tolerant mice); NOP antagonists give long-lasting analgesia and reduce tolerance, a possible future target
Sufentanil: fentanyl analogue, 5–10 times more potent than fentanyl; used for induction and maintenance
Hydromorphone: long-acting, for postoperative pain
Oral
100mg twice daily
Combination products (e.g. Anarex): three to four times daily
Anticholinergic: drowsiness, urinary retention, dry mouth
Used as a muscle relaxant
IV: 10mg in 1ml
Oral: immediate release (5-10mg) and sustained release (OxyContin)
Targin (oxycodone with naloxone): fixed prolonged-release tablets
5 mg/2.5 mg, 10 mg/5 mg, 20 mg/10 mg, 40 mg/20 mg
IV: dilute to 10ml to make 1mg/ml (as for morphine); give 1-2mg boluses
Oral
Paediatric oral: 0.1-0.2mg/kg Q6-8H (a bit less than morphine)
Opioid agonist, 1.5-2x more potent than morphine
Targin: naloxone has heavy first-pass metabolism, so no systemic effect, but acts locally on the gut (before the liver) to reduce constipation; oxycodone still acts systemically
Profile similar to morphine; some patients tolerate one better than the other
Cochrane 2017 (cancer pain): pain relief and overall adverse events similar to other strong opioids including morphine
Alternative to morphine for moderate to severe pain
Targin: severe pain with resistant constipation
May help postoperatively where constipation is a particular problem (haemorrhoidectomy, pelvic floor repair), despite being prolonged release
Oral bioavailability about 50% (85% in the Targin section of the note)
Metabolised to noroxycodone and oxymorphone
Medical grade: 99-99.5% pure
Made by fractional distillation of liquefied air, or by an oxygen concentrator
Concentrator: zeolite mesh adsorbs N2, leaving about 97% oxygen
Hospital supply: gas at room temperature and pressure, or refrigerated liquid
Gas: 2 banks of H cylinders (7080L each) on a manifold
Only 1 bank in use at a time
Manifold reduces cylinder pressure to line pressure and switches banks automatically when one is empty
Liquid: stored well below the critical temperature of -119°C (a gas can only be liquefied by pressure below its critical temperature)
Local backup: E cylinder (680L), fits most anaesthesia machines
Cylinder contents are judged by pressure, which falls in proportion to use
1000psig: E cylinder about half full (330L)
Bourdon gauge: flexible tube straightens under pressure, driving a gear that moves the pointer
Safety: pressure-relief valve set to rupture at 3300 psig (E cylinder walls withstand >5000); the yoke has parts made of Wood's metal, a low melting point alloy
Cardiovascular
Correcting hypoxaemia improves all cardiovascular variables
Prolonged 100% oxygen slightly lowers cardiac output and constricts coronary arteries
Lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure
Respiratory
Mild respiratory depression in healthy people at high concentration
In patients truly dependent on hypoxic drive, even modest concentrations may be fatal
Toxicity is due to free radicals
CNS: anxiety, nausea and seizures above 200 kPa partial pressure
Lung: lipid peroxidation of the alveolar capillary membrane; areas of collapse
Neonates: retrolental fibroplasia, possibly from vasoconstriction of developing retinal vessels
Total body water is high in neonates and infants
Term neonate: 75% of body weight (adult 60%); premature neonate up to 85%
Reaches adult values after 1 year of age
Leads to a larger volume of distribution for water-soluble drugs
Extracellular fluid is proportionately larger: 40% of body weight in the neonate, up to 60% in premature neonates (adult 20%)
Intracellular water rises as muscle mass increases
Infant water turnover is more than double the adult rate: about 40% of extracellular water
Due to higher evaporative loss (large surface area to body weight ratio) and higher respiratory water loss (higher minute ventilation)
Dehydration follows easily from reduced intake or extra losses because of:
High water turnover (evaporative and respiratory losses)
Poor renal concentrating ability
Anticipate deficits in:
Gastrointestinal losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, pancreatitis)
Ileus
Sepsis
Burns
Trauma
Postoperative bleeding
Hypovolaemia and dehydration are clinical diagnoses
Capillary refill time over 2 sec
Tachycardia (also from pain, fever, anxiety)
Oliguria
Cool peripheries, wider core-peripheral temperature gap
Sunken fontanelle, sunken eyes
Crying without tears, dry mucous membranes
Reduced consciousness: "the child that is confused might not be perfused"
Thready pulse
Hypotension is a late sign, often only after more than 30% of blood volume is lost
Shock: oxygen and nutrient demand of the cells exceeds delivery
Restore circulating volume with crystalloid (0.9% saline, Hartmann's) or colloid (plasma protein solution, Gelofusine, starch); blood products for major or ongoing loss
Replace extracellular losses with isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline, Hartmann's)
Burns, pyloric stenosis and diabetic ketoacidosis follow specific protocols
Estimated blood volume
Neonate 90 mL/kg
Infant 85 mL/kg
Child 80 mL/kg
Adult 70 mL/kg
Shock: 20 mL/kg boluses of crystalloid or colloid, then reassess
Not stable after 40, 60 and 80 mL/kg (depending on the situation and expected ongoing loss): consider intubation, inotropes and blood products
Blood after 15-20% of circulating volume lost
Fresh frozen plasma after 50% lost
Platelets after 100% lost
Rapid testing of specific factors with targeted replacement can reduce product use, risk and cost
Aims: replace any deficit, give maintenance, replace intraoperative losses
Preoperative deficit
Rarely an issue in elective cases: fasting times are short and children unable to drink get IV fluids
Non-elective deficits are usually corrected during preoperative resuscitation
Maintenance: dextrose-containing fluid or dextrose-free crystalloid (Hartmann's, 0.9% saline); dextrose-free is preferred
Glucose is usually unnecessary except in premature babies, neonates and other at-risk children (e.g. on parenteral nutrition)
Hypoglycaemia is rare in healthy children under anaesthesia; plasma glucose usually increases with the surgical stress response
4% or 5% dextrose fluids usually cause hyperglycaemia during surgery
Glucose fluids are isotonic in the bag but become hypotonic once the glucose is metabolised, so act as free water and risk hyponatraemia
Perioperative ADH release (stress, pain, hypovolaemia, drugs) lowers plasma sodium and osmolarity further
Children become hyponatraemic more readily than adults and suffer more CNS effects; now seen as a major perioperative risk
Intraoperative losses (exposure, handling, inflammation), guide by surgery type:
Superficial surgery: 1-3 ml/kg/h
Abdominal, chest or hip surgery: 3-4 ml/kg/h
Extensive abdominal surgery: 6-8 ml/kg/h
Most surgical losses are isotonic: replace with crystalloid, colloid or blood as needed

text: Some anaesthetists restrict postoperative maintenance to 50-75% of the calculated volume
The newborn's extracellular compartment is expanded; it contracts in the first few days with weight loss and negative water and sodium balance (normal)
Restrict fluid until this postnatal weight loss has happened; needs then rise to those of a growing infant
Water requirement rises over the first 4 days
Day 1: 60 mL/kg/day
Day 2: 90 mL/kg/day
Day 3: 120 mL/kg/day
Day 4: 150 mL/kg/day
Day 5 to 1 month: 150 mL/kg/day
Day 6 to 1 month (preterm): 180 ml/kg/day
Electrolytes (added)
Sodium 2-4 mmol/kg/day (stable, unlike water needs)
Dextrose
Usually 10% solution for maintenance
20% occasionally needed in septic or fluid-restricted neonates
Anaesthetist will push dextrose into the drip
Use the best weight (babies lose weight for 7 to 10 days after birth before regaining)
Caveats
After significant intrapartum stress, babies void late and need less fluid over the first 24-48 hours
Very small or immature infants under 1000 g have higher insensible losses

Based on a three-compartment model
V1 (central): plasma plus tissues that behave like plasma for that drug; loading bolus = target concentration x V1 (Cp x V1)

keo is found by experiment: peak effect occurs where the falling plasma curve after a bolus meets the rising effect-site curve; the trial keo whose effect-site curve matches plasma at the observed peak effect is taken as the real keo

Management
Review history, DM control and complications, anaesthetic chart (paraesthesia during spinal, hypotension, positioning) and operation notes (nerve injury, tourniquet time)
Full lower limb examination (sensory, motor, reflexes); upper limb and cranial nerves to exclude a central cause
Reassure and explain; discuss with surgeons; early nerve conduction studies and EMG; early neurology referral; follow-up alongside surgical review

Avoid GA (no anaesthesia or regional); avoid dehydration; acupuncture or acupressure; aromatherapy

Hydrogen nuclei (protons) spin and so create a magnetic field

Relaxation is measured two ways (T1 and T2)
T1 (longitudinal): time for protons to realign with the external magnetic field; fat bright, CSF dark

With ultrasound: at the elbow or mid-forearm, a thin bright structure lateral to the radial artery, above the radius
